title: The Power of Reverse Psychology
desc: Why does being told not to do something make us want it more? A calm, sourced long listen about psychological reactance, the quiet alarm that goes off when our freedom feels threatened: toddlers and forbidden toys, the Romeo and Juliet effect and its failed replication, censorship and warning labels, scarcity, signs that backfire, health messages that boomerang, white bears and ironic rebound, forbidden snacks, who reacts most, teenagers and autonomy, whether reverse psychology really works, why a sense of control matters, and how to persuade without pushing. It ends with a slow guided wind-down for sleep. Every claim comes from named studies, and the doubts are left in.
plan: b01: intro (the 'don't press the button' moment, Tom Sawyer's fence, Twain 1876); what reactance is (Brehm 1966; Brehm & Brehm 1981; Dillard & Shen 2005: anger + counter-arguing); tonight list
b02: forbidden toys (Brehm & Weinraub 1977 two-year-olds and barriers; Aronson & Carlsmith 1963 mild vs severe threat; Freedman 1965 weeks later)
b03: the Romeo and Juliet effect (Driscoll, Davis & Lipetz 1972) and its failed replication (Sinclair, Hood & Wright 2014; Sprecher & Felmlee 1992 network approval)
b04: censorship and forbidden information (Worchel & Arnold 1973; Worchel, Arnold & Baker 1975; Bushman & Stack 1996 forbidden-fruit warning labels)
b05: scarcity makes things precious (Worchel, Lee & Adewole 1975 cookie jars; Mazis, Settle & Leslie 1973 detergent ban in Miami)
b06: signs that backfire (Pennebaker & Sanders 1976 graffiti signs; Cialdini 2003 Petrified Forest signs as a different kind of backfire)
b07: health messages that boomerang (Grandpre et al. 2003; Miller et al. 2007 controlling language; Rains 2013 meta-analysis; Hornik et al. 2008 youth anti-drug campaign)
b08: rules we set for ourselves: white bears and ironic rebound (Wegner, Schneider, Carter & White 1987; Wegner 1994)
b09: forbidden snacks and children (Fisher & Birch 1999; Jansen, Mulkens & Jansen 2007 'do not eat the red ones')
b10: who reacts most (Hong & Page 1989 scale; Hong et al. 1994 age; Jonas et al. 2009 culture and group freedom)
b11: teenagers and autonomy (Van Petegem, Soenens, Vansteenkiste & Beyers 2015; Deci & Ryan 2000 self-determination)

b12: does reverse psychology actually work? (MacDonald, Nail & Harper 2011; Frankl's paradoxical intention; Ascher & Turner 1979; Shoham-Salomon & Rosenthal 1987; Friestad & Wright 1994 persuasion knowledge)
b13: why a sense of control matters (Langer & Rodin 1976; Rodin & Langer 1977; Iyengar & Lepper 2000; Scheibehenne et al. 2010 meta-analysis)
b14: persuading without pushing (Gueguen & Pascual 2000 'but you are free'; Carpenter 2013 meta-analysis; Miller & Rollnick motivational interviewing; Moyer-Guse 2008 stories)
b15: noticing reactance in yourself (Petty & Cacioppo 1979 forewarning; McGuire 1961 inoculation; pausing before the 'you can't tell me' reflex)
b16: takeaways, callback to Tom Sawyer's fence, start of the wind-down
b17: wind-down: nothing you have to do tonight
b18: wind-down: an evening walk with no rules
b19: wind-down: a quiet garden at night
b20: wind-down, goodnight, end (next: Why Social Media Is So Hard to Put Down)
